items.summary: Manchester United manager Michael Carrick is under growing pressure, but club legend Wayne Rooney takes aim at players.

items.summary: Al Jazeera interviews Fatih Birol in Berlin as the Iran war disrupts global energy supplies.

items.summary: High winds propelled the blaze across the army base in Wainwright, killing four soldiers and injuring dozens more.

items.summary: Karachi's last two African elephants remain in captivity. Their sisters are already dead. Will they survive?

items.title: Israel preparing full lockdown of occupied West Bank after Hebron gunfight
items.summary: Clampdown comes as Israeli pogroms heighten tensions and spread violence across Palestinian territory.

items.title: France: 1 killed, 4 wounded after shooting near Paris
items.summary: French police have arrested a suspect after gunshots were fired in a town in the suburbs of Paris on Friday. One person was killed and four others were wounded in the shooting. The motive was not immediately clear.

items.title: Sri Lanka: Death of iconic elephant raises habitat concerns
items.summary: The death of what was thought to be Sri Lanka’s largest elephant has drawn attention to human-elephant conflict in rural communities. The island country sees a high number of deadly encounters.

items.title: Greece joins countries putting age-limits on social media, banning access for kids under 15
items.summary: Greece has passed legislation banning social media access for children under 15. New rules will come into effect on January 1, 2027, and are designed to protect children's mental health.

items.title: Germany news: Wadephul says 'threat of famine' due to ongoing wars
items.summary: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul is joining counterparts in Turkey for discussions on a range of interlinked geopolitical crises. Back in Germany, the Bavarian CSU party begins its two-day conference in Munich.

items.title: Israel preparing 'full closure' of West Bank, Netanyahu says
items.summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel is shutting down the occupied West Bank after having prevented a "major attack."

items.title: South Korea proposes military talks with North again
items.summary: South Korea is attempting to mutually determine the land border with North Korea amid military incidents and escalating tensions.

items.title: Germany sit out FIFA Under-15 World Cup as Russia return
items.summary: Germany is one a handful of FIFA's 211 nations to refuse an invitation to play at the inaugural Under-15 World Cup. The tournament will also mark Russia's return to the FIFA fold.

items.title: Taiwan braces as El Nino-supercharged Typhoon Champi approaches island
items.summary: One person has died and thousands have been evacuated as Taiwan prepares for a possible direct hit. Though no longer a "super" typhoon, Champi is still packing winds of nearly 200 kmh and will bring torrential rain.

items.title: Musk's Starshield system 'back' in Ukraine, says Trump
items.summary: US President Trump has said he wouldn't comment on who called for capping Ukraine's Starshield access but added that Elon Musk had "put it back." His account was rejected by Ukraine, which says nothing has changed.

items.title: Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like
items.summary: Names are central to our identity, so what happens when that name is a source of ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

items.title: India news: Protesters march to Election Commission demanding CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation
items.summary: A coalition of students, farmers and civil society groups have joined calls for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over India's voter roll revision exercise. DW has more.

items.title: Serbia: Tens of thousands rally ahead of elections
items.summary: After two years of student-led protests, Serbia will soon vote in what observers describe as a referendum-like snap election pitting strongman Aleksandar Vucic against the student movement.

items.title: Airbnb scraps guest checkout chores such as cleaning
items.summary: Under new rules, guests will no longer have to do tasks that cleaners would normally handle. Hosts can now only make "reasonable" requests, such as leaving dirty dishes in the sink and sorting trash from recycling.

items.title: Tibet earthquake kills at least 16 people, injures dozens: state media
items.summary: A powerful magnitude 7 earthquake has struck Tibet in southwestern China, official media reported. Chinese state TV said it's the strongest quake to hit the remote Himalayan region in five years.

items.title: Poland: Thousands protest for more abortion rights
items.summary: Thousands rallied across Poland to demand abortion rights six years after a landmark court ruling tightened restrictions. The country has one of the strictest abortion rules in all of Europe.

items.title: Albania's student protests are only getting bigger
items.summary: As police try to suppress anti-corruption protests by young Albanians, Prime Minister Edi Rama is claiming that "antifa" is behind the unrest. Few are buying that explanation.

items.title: Lina Attalah: Mada Masr journalist sent for trial in Egypt
items.summary: Lina Attalah, who is accused of managing a website without a license, will go to court next week. Mada Masr has published reporting critical of Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi's government.

items.title: 96% of world's coral reefs face critical risk of collapse, IUCN warns
items.summary: Almost all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs are at risk of collapse by 2075, with climate change the biggest threat. A new study found that 96% of reef systems are critically endangered.

items.title: Canada's Mark Carney visits Turkey to boost trade ties
items.summary: It's the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey. Canada and Turkey upgraded their relations to a "strategic partnership" as Canada seeks to diversify trade beyond the US.

items.title: France's Macron says 'illegitimate' protests will be banned in coming days
items.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron vowed to ban unauthorized protests after France was rocked by violence and looting. As anger over public services and the cost of living grows, authorities are bracing for more protests.

items.title: Are the French police the most violent in the EU?
items.summary: As protests continue in France, the French police are under scrutiny after new allegations of police brutality. The force has a bigger arsenal than most in Europe.

items.title: Ukraine: Life near the front line in Sloviansk
items.summary: As Russian continues to attack Sloviansk in eastern Ukraine, thousands of residents refuse to leave or struggle to find a way out. For many, poverty, family ties and beloved pets make evacuation painfully difficult.

items.title: Can Germany overhaul its economy before AfD grows stronger?
items.summary: Conflicts, rising costs and Chinese competition are testing Germany's economic model like never before. Which new sectors could revive growth and contain the far-right AfD, whose support has grown larger than ever?

items.title: Harry Kane: Ballon d’Or for Bayern Munich striker?
items.summary: Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane is the clear front-runner for football's most prestigious individual prize, which will be awarded on Monday. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.

items.title: Bulgaria: Concerns about security in the Black Sea dominate presidential election campaign
items.summary: Bulgaria's presidential election campaign has been shaped by recent drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea and the government's reduced support for Ukraine, making foreign policy a key factor in the first round.

items.title: EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm
items.summary: The European Union wants to relax rules for pesticides, saying it will be easier for farmers to adopt more environmentally friendly options. But health and environmental experts say the risks are far too great.

items.title: Germany news: AfD's Weidel calls for major EU reforms
items.summary: Far-right Alternative for Germany co-leader Alice Weidel reveals the party's plan to reform the EU. Meanwhile, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was in Berlin to talk to developers and investors. DW has more.

items.title: Trump, Putin and Xi at one table, without Ukraine. What Moscow wants from the proposal and why Beijing might agree.
items.summary: Moscow is pushing for a summit with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, without Kyiv or the EU. What does Russia hope to gain, and why might China be willing to take part?

items.title: Raids at far-right group's offices at European Parliament
items.summary: Authorities searched the Patriots for Europe's European Parliament offices in a long-running funding inquiry. The group says the charges pertain to its predecessor and there is "no legal continuity" between the two.

items.title: Russia arrests German man, calls him a Ukraine 'mercenary'
items.summary: Russian FSB agents have arrested a German national and accused him of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine's military. They claim he deserted over unpaid wages and say he was a sniper who once served in the Bundeswehr.

items.title: Russia frees jailed American Stephen Hubbard during Witkoff talks
items.summary: During talks between Vladimir Putin and Steve Witkoff, Putin announced that jailed American Stephen Hubbard had been released. The Kremlin also said Russia was "in principle" ready to resume trilateral talks next month.

items.title: US sanctions target Iran's rail sector as Tehran shifts cargo from sea routes to overland corridors
items.summary: As US sanctions expand to Iran's rail sector, Tehran is relying more heavily on overland links with China and Central Asia. But capacity constraints, delays and costs limit rail's ability to replace maritime trade.

items.title: Football: German coach Hürzeler flying high in Premier League
items.summary: Fabian Hürzeler is younger than his star player, a fellow Premier League German. But, contrary to his reputation in his homeland, Hürzeler has become a popular figure both on and off the pitch in England.

items.title: Rising emissions and temperatures: The cost of Trump's climate retreat is now clear
items.summary: The world is set to breach the critical 1.5-degree temperature limit, with Donald Trump's US withdrawal from climate action worsening the outlook, according to a UN report. But there is a small silver lining.

items.title: New EU plan for Arctic warily eyes influence of Russia, US
items.summary: The EU unveiled its priorities in the Arctic as it vies with Russia, China and the US for influence. EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said drone incursions, GPS jamming and cable sabotage undermine Arctic security.

items.title: Germany news: Hackers release AfD party emails
items.summary: Germany's far-right AfD has launched an inquiry after the release of thousands of emails following a cyberattack. Also, investors pledged billions for Germany at a major summit in Berlin. DW has more news from Germany.

items.title: Wagner brothers begin new NBA chapter on different paths
items.summary: After five years, brothers Franz and Moritz Wagner are no longer playing together for the Orlando Magic. In the new NBA season, their separation will likely mean the new "German" team is the Charlotte Hornets.

items.title: Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand
items.summary: Increasing amounts of US capital are flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses. As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming acquisition targets.

items.title: Brutal, revolutionary empire builder: Genghis Khan's legacy
items.summary: Berlin is host to a major exhibition on the founder of the Mongol Empire and his successors. Here's how Genghis Khan disrupted the course of history.

items.title: Bulgaria seeks suspects in Germany after Starlink sabotage
items.summary: A Bulgarian court has issued arrest warrants for two young German nationals suspected of setting fire to Starlink antennas. The case is reminiscent of another in Poland, which Warsaw says was orchestrated by Russia.

items.title: Germany news: Emergency at Leipzig airport sparked by novice driver
items.summary: Two men breached a fence at the Leipzig/Halle airport while practicing for a driving test. Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced an industrial AI partnership with Nvidia. DW has more.

items.title: The homeless man living in front of a London mega-mansion
items.summary: Anders Fernstedt lives in London without any money. The Swedish native has built a most unusual home under the porch of a house worth over €200 million. How did that happen?

items.title: What Earth's sixth mass extinction event means for humans
items.summary: Human activity is driving plants and animals to extinction at an unprecedented rate. As countries meet in Armenia to discuss ways to reverse nature loss, DW reveals how declining biodiversity is already harming people.

items.title: France: Young voters blase about Glucksmann's Socialists
items.summary: Raphael Glucksmann wants to lead France's Socialists to power without working with the left-populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, who is particularly popular with young voters. How can the center-left candidate win them over?

items.title: Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?
items.summary: Would you work 12 hours straight? The CDU/CSU and SPD are locked in a dispute over reforms to the Working Hours Act. Workplace flexibility, collective bargaining agreements and worker protection rules are at stake.

items.title: How reliant is Ukraine on the US-controlled Starlink internet service?
items.summary: Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down?

items.title: Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections
items.summary: Opposition parties still control the Czech Senate, in a major blow to Prime Minister Andrej Babis' and his governing coalition.

items.title: How big is Russia's threat against Germany?
items.summary: Experts believe that, so far, Germany has been ill-prepared — both militarily and mentally — for Russian provocations. They also warn against the idea that ending support for Ukraine would make Germany safer.

items.title: China's influence in the gaming industry is growing
items.summary: Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the world.

items.title: Russia wants blackout in Ukraine as winter comes — Zelenskyy
items.summary: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy says Russia is trying to cut electricity and heating to civilians ahead of winter. He also called the US president's waiver of new sanctions on Moscow a boost for Vladimir Putin.

items.title: France: Protesters clash with police in nationwide protests, amid rising social polarization
items.summary: Unrest broke out in parts of France as students, trade unionists and Yellow Vest activists took to the streets to protest high prices and inequality. Police arrested over 1,000 people amid chaotic scenes.

items.title: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy speaks at EU summit amid spat with Donald Trump
items.summary: EU leaders reaffirmed support for Ukraine at the Brussels summit. But souring relations with the US over Russia and Starlink and a big hole in the budget will make for a difficult winter for Ukraine.

items.title: Hijab ban at schools in Azerbaijan: What's behind the rare wave of protests?
items.summary: Girls wearing headscarves have been turned away from schools in Azerbaijan, triggering unusual protests involving children. The government rules do not mention hijabs. Why are schools enforcing unwritten rules?

items.title: The Bundestag has debated the genocide Germany carried out in Namibia a century ago. But will it spur progress on addressing colonial crimes?
items.summary: Opposition parties have forced a debate in the Bundestag on the early-20th-century genocide Germany carried out in Namibia. Will this finally spur progress in addressing colonial crimes?

items.title: Albania: Students demand political change and resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama
items.summary: Empty lecture halls, burning buildings and demands for change: Albanian students are spearheading a protest movement that has become the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama in years.

items.title: The EU wants an AI revolution. But on whose terms?
items.summary: As the US and China race ahead, the European Union seeks to boost its economy with AI. Can it compete while protecting workers, safety and the climate?

items.title: Italy cuts air traffic in half amid data transmission issue
items.summary: Citing problems with the data transmission network, Italian authorities have drastically reduced the volume of flights in their airspace. The ENAV authority ruled out malicious activity and said flights remained safe.

items.title: Who was Eva Mamlok? Berlin square renamed after Jewish anti-fascist resistance fighter
items.summary: She started taking action against Hitler as a teenager and never stopped until her death in a concentration camp. Berlin's Blücherplatz is now being renamed after her.

items.title: EU promotes sovereign, trusted AI as it struggles to catch US and China
items.summary: At an international AI summit in Dublin, EU leaders promoted trusted and independent artificial intelligence. Critics question whether the bloc can close the gap with the US and China while maintaining strict regulation.

items.title: Formula One in Rwanda: Sportswashing claims vs. hopes for African legacy
items.summary: Formula One will return to Africa for the first time since 1993. There is concern Rwanda are using it as another sportswashing opportunity, but there is also hope the event's legacy can impact wider African society.

items.title: Police raid the major pro-opposition Halk TV channel in Turkey
items.summary: Turkish police raided the Istanbul headquarters of an important pro-opposition television station on Wednesdazy, the day that jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu was set to start his defense against corruption charges.

items.title: Resignation of Bärbel Bas shines light on harsh era of German politics
items.summary: German Labor Minister Bärbel Bas has stepped down, citing her need to grieve a loved one and leave behind the harsh realities of government. So how did German politics get so heated?

items.title: AI-assisted dying? Doris Dörrie's new film addresses prospect of care robots
items.summary: While the world debates the dangers of artificial intelligence, filmmaker Doris Dörrie explores how humanoid robots could change the way we deal with aging, caregiving and how people choose to die.

items.title: Thousands of German gamblers could sue for their money back
items.summary: German gamblers may finally be able to beat the house, thanks to new court rulings in the EU and in Germany. The decisions could help gambling addicts — but the legal road might be difficult.

items.title: Germany news: Train station alcohol ban comes into force
items.summary: Consuming alcohol is no longer permitted at train stations in Germany, to improve the lot of travelers and staff alike. Coalition talks are restarting in Berlin, and an inmate is loose in Essen.

items.title: Brazil's elections matter for the planet. This is why
items.summary: Brazil is heading back to the polls, but the impact could be felt worldwide. With the Amazon vital to the health of the planet, the election could help shape its future.

items.title: Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums
items.summary: From action cameras and smartphones to EVs and robot vacuums, Chinese brands are gaining ground worldwide, despite privacy and security concerns. What's driving their rise, and can European rivals keep up?

items.title: Manchester City, the UAE and the UK's OM in a political tangle
items.summary: Nearly 20 years after arriving in England, Manchester City's UAE owners could exit amid cheating charges. That would pose a challenge for a city — and prime minister — closely tied to Abu Dhabi.

items.title: Nord Stream trial opens in Germany, defense seeks dismissal
items.summary: Serhii Kuznietsov is accused of attacking civilian infrastructure in the 2022 sabotage of the Russian gas pipeline to Germany. His lawyers called Nord Stream a military target, and said their client is sworn to secrecy.

items.title: Germany's far-right AfD forges a pro-Russia alliance with the BSW
items.summary: In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD and BSW are joining forces to push for negotiations with Moscow. What is driving this rapprochement?

items.title: Trump's diesel deal with Russia is unlikely to significantly lower global fuel prices despite expectations of rapid relief
items.summary: As the world's largest diesel exporter, the US benefits from high prices. At home, however, consumers are feeling the strain of rising living costs. Why Donald Trump's deal with Russia is unlikely to change that.

items.title: Nord Stream: Germany puts suspected Ukrainian pipeline saboteur on trial
items.summary: A Ukrainian citizen faces court in Hamburg, accused of attacking the Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022. It raises questions about Kyiv's possible role in the explosions. German support for Ukraine is also under scrutiny.

items.title: Do non-German nationals commit more crimes than Germans?
items.summary: People without German passports appear more frequently in German police crime statistics than German nationals. A new study explains why.

items.title: FIFPRO report highlights growing pains in women's football
items.summary: Expected global revenue of over $1 billion and new faces at the U17 World Cup show women's football is booming, but a recent report also highlights need for better structures globally.

items.title: The hidden treasure in discarded wearable and fast tech
items.summary: Sales of fast tech like mini fans and disposable e-vapes, as well as wearable health tech such as heart monitors and smartwatches are soaring. They're creating a new e-waste problem but are full of hidden treasure.

items.title: Formula 1: Rwanda to bring sport back to Africa
items.summary: The last time Formula 1 hosted a race in Africa was way back in 1993. But a new track in Rwanda is set to host a Grand Prix in "the early 2030s," continuing the country’s investment in international sport.

items.title: Germany's China calculation shifts as import pressures eclipse export benefits
items.summary: Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.

items.title: 125 years of Thomas Mann's 'Buddenbrooks'
items.summary: This over 1,000-page masterpiece offers a panoramic view of society in the 19th century and exposes the collapse of a merchant family: unrecognized sons, disillusioned daughters and the loss of middle-class ideals.

items.title: Germany: Labor Minister's resignation puts a spotlight on cracks within the government
items.summary: Following the sudden resignation of Bärbel Bas as Labor Minister and co-chair of the Social Democratic Party, accusations are flying in Chancellor Merz's coalition government.

items.title: Pope lung nodule: Could it be cancer?
items.summary: The case of Pope Leo shows how small lung nodules are often found during routine health checks. Quick treatment is generally advised before nodules can grow to become larger life-threatening masses.

items.title: Germany's women: Ena Mahmutovic makes her case to become Germany's next No.1 goalkeeper
items.summary: Germany's win against Australia saw Ena Mahmutovic excel in goal. The 22-year-old Bayern Munich goalkeeper is considered the successor to Ann-Katrin Berger and is making a name for herself.

items.title: How green is Europe's urban public transport? A data-driven reality check
items.summary: Greener buses and cleaner fleets are reshaping public transport across Europe. But are cities moving fast enough to meet their zero-emission goals?

items.title: UK students call for school uniforms to be banned in pornography
items.summary: Short skirts, knee-high socks, white blouses: Girls' school uniform items are widely used as costumes in pornographic videos. As students experience harassment, a group wants to change that.

items.title: German 'lawfare': When lawsuits become a political weapon
items.summary: The Left Party is suing two government ministers for accusing them of antisemitism, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz has been sued several times by various parties. Is German politics descending into "lawfare?"

items.title: Germany's population is shrinking, but not everywhere
items.summary: By 2045, Germany will have more older people, fewer workers and a smaller population overall. Yet some regions will defy this trend. Their success depends on how much they have to offer.

items.title: 'Ragebait' is the 2026 German Youth Word of the Year
items.summary: Already named the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year, "rage bait" has also been widely adopted in German slang.

items.title: Operations Plan Germany: How the Bundeswehr trains for NATO collective defense
items.summary: How prepared is Germany for national defense? The answer lies in the Operations Plan Germany. Military exercises such as "Red Storm Charlie" are designed to put these preparations to the test in realistic scenarios.

items.title: Author or artificial intelligence? Literature in crisis
items.summary: AI is a hot topic at this year's Frankfurt Book Fair. An international literary scandal has raised questions about machine-generated texts.

items.title: Art for freedom: Maria Kalesnikava in Bonn
items.summary: The Belarusian musician and civil rights activist Maria Kalesnikava held the keynote speech on the importance of art at the 2026 Beethovenfest in Bonn. She also visited DW.

items.title: World Cup 2034: Does Saudi Arabia shelving Neom Stadium spell trouble?
items.summary: Since winning the right to hold the 2034 World Cup unopposed, Saudi Arabia has been pulling away from sport. With reports that its most ambitious stadium project will be abandoned, what does this mean for the World Cup?

items.title: Finland, the world's happiest nation, faces a glum winter
items.summary: Finns have many reasons to feel content, but the country's pile of debt is not one of them. Russia's war in Ukraine has added to the fiscal burden. Can the Nordic nation absorb another shock?

items.title: 2026 Nobel Prize winner Anne Carson: Where to start reading
items.summary: The works of this year's Nobel Prize-winning poet and essayist Anne Carson can feel slightly daunting. Here are some keys to understanding her universe.

items.title: Early-onset cancer rising worldwide: Causes, risk, prevention
items.summary: Across Latin America, early-onset cancer rates have risen, especially of bowel, breast and cervical cancers. But it is a worldwide trend.

items.title: Germany news: UK's Burnham visits Berlin for talks with Merz
items.summary: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is visiting Berlin to launch a new bilateral treaty and hold talks with Chancellor Friedrich Merz. President Steinmeier is on a state visit to France.

items.title: How a multibillion-dollar oilfield has ignited the UK-Argentina feud over the Falklands
items.summary: Argentina and the UK once fought a war over the Falkland Islands. Now, the multibillion-dollar Sea Lion oil project has reignited old tensions, with Buenos Aires seeking to put a stop to the plans.

items.title: Nobel Prize in literature goes to Canada's Anne Carson
items.summary: Carson won for her "bold and inventive oeuvre." The decorated poet and essayist is known for her reverence for Latin and Greek classics.

items.title: '90s art scene in the UK: An international, edgy trendsetter
items.summary: The 1990s are remembered for Brit-pop and provocative fashion, but beyond the nostalgia, it was a decade of cultural experimentation and social change. Tate Britain's new exhibition looks past the familiar icons.

items.title: Nobel Prize in chemistry goes to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai
items.summary: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for their groundbreaking discoveries related to the origin of chirality and life's building blocks.

items.title: Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What we know about the disease
items.summary: After a worker at a Russian plague research institute in Siberia died October 2, 2026, nearly 200 of her contacts were under medical observation. But authorities there denied pneumonic plague had caused the death.

items.title: Ronaldo stays on under cloud as Messi exits internationals
items.summary: Just hours before Lionel Messi played his last match for Argentina, Cristiano Ronaldo posted his latest salvo in a row with Portugal. Ronaldo wants to play on despite the troubles, while Messi bathed in adulation.

items.title: Nobelitis — How winning a Nobel Prize can give you delusions of grandeur
items.summary: After being chosen for one of the world's most prestigious awards, some Nobel laureates lose touch with reality and suddenly start spouting unscientific nonsense. They're afflicted by what some have called "Nobelitis."

items.title: Emerging economies are embracing solar power and skipping fossil fuels much faster than Europe or the US
